questions.q: What does "crowding" mean as a cause of strategy decay?
options: Too many unrelated strategies running on the same server
Other market participants finding and trading the same pattern, which competes away the edge and can worsen execution for everyone trading it
A strategy trading too many different asset classes at once
A broker limiting how many orders a strategy can place per day
questions.explain: Crowding happens when other participants discover and act on the same pattern a strategy exploits, competing away the original edge — one of the lesson's three named causes of decay, alongside regime change and structural market change.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend a rolling-window Sharpe ratio instead of relying on a single whole-period Sharpe ratio to detect decay?
options: A single whole-period Sharpe ratio can blend a strong first half and a weak, decayed second half into an unremarkable average, hiding the decay entirely
Rolling windows are always mathematically identical to the whole-period Sharpe ratio
Whole-period Sharpe ratios cannot be computed for strategies longer than one year
Rolling windows eliminate the need to ever compute Sharpe ratios at all
questions.explain: In the lesson's example, the strategy's rolling Sharpe fell from 2.35 to 0.17 over the back half of the sample — a clear decay that a single Sharpe ratio averaged over the whole period would have obscured by blending the strong and weak periods together.

questions.q: Why does the lesson's retirement-review rule require multiple consecutive below-threshold checks (e.g., 3 monthly checks) rather than acting on a single bad window?
options: Because requiring multiple checks guarantees the strategy will never be flagged
To avoid reacting to a single noisy bad window, given the same sampling-uncertainty concerns raised in Lesson 25 about short-sample noise
Because broker APIs require a minimum of three consecutive signals before accepting a retirement decision
Multiple checks are only needed for strategies with negative Sharpe ratios
questions.explain: A single rolling-window Sharpe reading below the threshold could just be short-term noise, echoing Lesson 25's warning about sampling uncertainty. Requiring several consecutive below-threshold checks distinguishes a sustained decline from a temporary rough patch.

questions.q: What is the key tradeoff in choosing how sensitive a retirement-review rule should be?
options: There is no tradeoff; more sensitive is always strictly better
A more sensitive rule risks false alarms on short-lived rough patches, while a less sensitive rule risks giving up more capital to a genuinely decayed strategy before flagging it
Sensitivity only affects how the rule is coded, not its real-world outcomes
The tradeoff only matters for strategies trading more than one asset
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this as a real design tradeoff: reacting faster risks false alarms from short-term noise, while reacting slower means more capital is lost to a strategy that has actually decayed before the review is triggered.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does a "retirement review" flag actually mean for a strategy?
options: The strategy must be immediately and permanently deleted with no further analysis

It triggers a deliberate evaluation that could lead to pausing and re-paper-testing, reducing size while investigating, or genuinely retiring and documenting the strategy — but should never be ignored
It means the strategy's code should be left running unchanged while the team waits to see if performance improves
It automatically increases the strategy's position size to compensate for the decay
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes retirement review from automatic shutdown: the outcome could be pausing for re-testing, resizing during investigation, or formal retirement with documentation — but leaving a flagged strategy running unchanged and unaddressed is exactly the failure mode monitoring is meant to prevent.
